newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher, recover after ECI.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher, recover after ECI.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries rebounded from early losses to close higher on Tuesday, as the market, hoping for a weaker report as had been the case previously, overcame somewhat troublesome employment costs data.
As a result, yields fell to their lowest levels since right after Thanksgiving.
The 30-year bond ended at 103-8/32, up 11/32 from Monday. Its yield edged down to 6.38 percent from 6.41 percent, its lowest level since closing at 6.37 percent on December 3.
"It seems like there continues to be strong positive signals in the market," said Doug Gray, a trader at Zions First National Bank.

Early in the session, the Labor Department reported that the employment cost index rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter, after a 0.6 percent gain in the first quarter. Labor costs in the second quarter were up 2.8 percent, year-over-year.
Although the number was as expected, the market had hoped for a weaker than consensus figure like the prior few reports.
"This number in the past has been so surprisingly friendly that since today was as expected the market said, 'how can you do it to us?'" noted one trader at a West Coast primary dealership.
The disappointment prompted profit-taking and hedge fund selling, since the market was said to have been mostly long in anticipation of a weaker ECI report.
Helping to push Treasuries even lower was hedging against spread products and swaption of the Long Island Lighting Co's rate lock deal.
But short-covering, in the wake of a drop in the Conference Board's July consumer confidence index to 126.5 from June's 129.9, took the market off its lows.

Flows from mortgage backed securities aided the Treasuries' rally, and the market rose to session highs late in the day after a number of key resistence levels were broken: below 6.40 percent on the 30-year bond yield, below 6.10 percent on the 10-year note and above 115-28/32 on the September bond contract.
"Technicals are ruling the roost," said one trader.

Also of interest, but having little impact, was the budget pact between the White House and Congressional leaders, which included about $90 billion in tax cuts and holds appropraitions increases to an average 0.5 percent a year.

Attention shifts to supply, in which the Treasury will anounce details of next week's quarterly refunding Wednesday afternoon. Analysts expect about $38 billion of three- and 10-year notes and 30-year bonds to be sold.

In late trading, the 10-year note was up 8/32 at 103-27/32 to yield 6.10 percent. The five-year note was at 101-1/32, up 5/32, to yield 5.99 percent, and the two-year note was up 3/32 at 100-5/32 to yield 5.79 percent.
Three-month bills were unchanged at 5.09 percent. Six-month bills were down one basis point at 5.12 percent and year bills were down four basis points at 5.17 percent.
